title: Chang'an Gazetteer
subtitle: Song Minqiu · The Earliest Surviving Chang'an Local Gazetteer · A Complete Picture of Tang Chang'an
description: Song Minqiu (1019–1079), courtesy name Cidao, was a native of Zhaozhou Pingji (modern Zhaoxian, Hebei), a renowned historian and bibliophile of the Northern Song. He extensively collected Tang dynasty documents and completed the twenty-volume Chang'an Gazetteer during the Xining era, comprehensively recording the palaces, wards, temples, residences, and山川 of Tang Chang'an. It is the earliest and most complete surviving local gazetteer of Chang'an and the most important primary source for studying the complete picture of Tang Chang'an. This route follows the Chang'an of Song Minqiu's writing, seeking the vestiges of the Great Tang in today's Xi'an.

route.title: Chang'an Gazetteer: Song Minqiu's Tang Chang'an — A Thousand-Year Capital's Restoration on Paper
route.intro:
Chang'an, the ancient capital. The Xianyang of Qin, the Chang'an of Han, the Daxing of Sui, which the Tang used as their capital.
Song Minqiu was born into a scholarly family — his father Song Shou was chancellor to Emperor Renzong of Song, with thirty thousand volumes in the family library. He grew up in a sea of books, possessing an almost obsessive passion for historical geography. By the Northern Song, the Tang capital Chang'an was already abandoned — ever since 904, when Zhu Wen forced Emperor Zhaozong of Tang to move the capital to Luoyang and 'destroyed Chang'an's palaces, government offices, and civilian houses, taking their timber down the Wei River,' Chang'an had become a city of ruins. But Song Minqiu refused to accept this. He spent half a lifetime gathering every Tang document he could find — the Old and New Tang Histories, the Record of the Two Capitals, the Guanzhong Record, Tang dynasty notebooks — taking a city that no longer existed as his subject, ward by ward, lane by lane, restoring its appearance. His Chang'an Gazetteer tells future generations: Chang'an is not a myth. Where the palace was, where the market was, which street a certain poet lived on — all are documented. Let us open the Chang'an Gazetteer and enter that Great Tang Chang'an, which can only be seen in its entirety on paper.

stops.title: Stop 1: Daming Palace — The Glorious Stage Where Ten Thousand Nations Paid Homage
stops.content: The Chang'an Gazetteer's record of Daming Palace is the most detailed of all palaces. Song Minqiu wrote: 'Daming Palace is southeast of the Forbidden Park, to the south adjoining the northern side of the capital city, to the west adjoining the northeastern corner of the palace city.' — he precisely gave the location and extent of Daming Palace. This palace was first built in the eighth year of the Zhenguan era (634), constructed by Li Shimin as a summer retreat for his father Li Yuan, and later became the most important political center of the Tang dynasty. Song Minqiu listed the halls and pavilions of Daming Palace in detail: Hanyuan Hall was the venue for grand state ceremonies, Xuanzheng Hall was where the emperor conducted daily court, Zichen Hall was the inner court hall, Linde Hall was where grand banquets were held — 'east and west towers before the hall, a pavilion to the south, and towers to the east and west.' He wrote: 'The staircase of Hanyuan Hall is forty feet high' — that towering visual effect evokes the splendor described in the line: 'The nine-latticed heavenly portal opens wide the palace, and ten thousand nations in court robes bow before the imperial crown.' Today, Daming Palace has become the Daming Palace Site Park — the platform of Hanyuan Hall still stands ten meters high. Standing atop it and gazing out, you can almost see the magnificent scene of envoys from ten thousand nations lining up for court. Song Minqiu's Chang'an Gazetteer provided the most precise 'navigation' for today's archaeological work. The accuracy of Song Minqiu's account of Daming Palace has been repeatedly verified in millennia-spanning archaeology. He wrote: 'Hanyuan Hall has Qifeng and Xiangluan pavilions to left and right, and a Dragon-Tail Staircase beneath the hall' — the 1959 archaeological excavation fully confirmed this record, and the three-tiered ascending steps of the Dragon-Tail Staircase remain clearly visible today. He also recorded that Linde Hall 'measures one hundred and thirty paces from north to south, and seventy paces from east to west' — in today's figures, Linde Hall is about 130 meters wide and 70 meters deep, with a total area of 9,000 square meters, three times the size of the Forbidden City's Hall of Supreme Harmony. 'With a gallery in front, a pavilion behind, a tower to the east, and a building to the west' — this layout of enclosure on four sides later influenced the entire East Asian palace architectural system, from Japan's Heijokyo to Korea's Silla palaces, all showing the shadow of Daming Palace. Though Daming Palace's life lasted only a little over 270 years, its aesthetic genes live on in Chinese architecture. Standing on the Hanyuan Hall site and looking north, the水面 of Taiye Pool still shimmers — it was here that Emperor Minghuang of Tang and Yang Guifei went boating, and where Li Bai, drunk, wrote 'Clouds call to mind her robes, flowers her face.' Though Song Minqiu's Chang'an Gazetteer was written amid ruins, the Daming Palace in his pages is not a ruin — it is a complete and vibrant heart of the Great Tang, beating on paper for a millennium without pause.

stops.title: Stop 2: Xingqing Palace — The Royal Garden by Dragon Pond
stops.content: Xingqing Palace was one of the three great palaces of Tang Chang'an, located inside Chunming Gate. Song Minqiu recorded in the Chang'an Gazetteer: 'Xingqing Palace is east of the Imperial City, established in the early Kaiyuan era.' This palace was the former residence of Li Longji, Emperor Xuanzong of Tang, when he was a prince. After he ascended the throne, he expanded it into an imperial palace, spending the most beautiful time of his life there with Yang Guifei. Song Minqiu described Xingqing Palace's layout in detail: to the south were Xingqing Hall and Datong Hall, to the north was Dragon Pond — 'Dragon Pond is within Xingqing Palace, covering several qing.' Dragon Pond was the soul of Xingqing Palace — Xuanzong and his consort went boating on the pond, and the Aloes Pavilion on its shore was where Li Bai wrote 'Clouds call to mind her robes, flowers her face.' The palace also contained the famous Hall of Diligent Government — Xuanzong personally inscribed the plaque, expressing his intention to govern diligently and love the people. Today, Xingqing Palace Park has been built on the site. Though the pavilions and towers are reconstructions, the location of Dragon Pond has not changed — the willows on its southern shore still sway in the spring breeze, just as Song Minqiu wrote in his book. Xingqing Palace carries the most romantic and the saddest memories of the Great Tang. Song Minqiu recorded: 'In the sixteenth year of the Kaiyuan era, Xuanzong moved his court to Xingqing Palace, conducting affairs of state here' — from that year on, Xingqing Palace replaced Daming Palace as the power center of the Tang empire. The Aloes Pavilion witnessed the romance of Xuanzong and Yang Guifei — 'The consort excelled at singing and dancing, and would perform the Rainbow Skirt and Feathered Coat Melody in the pavilion, with the palace maidens imitating her, calling it the "Realm of Romance."' But good times did not last — in the fifteenth year of the Tianbao era (756), when An Lushan's rebel army approached Tong Pass, Xuanzong boarded his carriage to flee westward from Xingqing Palace, 'departing before dawn, more than half of the hundred officials unable to follow.' This palace, which had borne the songs of a golden age, became in one night the turning point of the Tang empire's decline. Though Xingqing Palace no longer stands, its site is an important component of the Sui Daxing and Tang Chang'an City Site. This Sui-Tang capital covered 84 square kilometers, six times larger than the contemporary city of Baghdad, the largest capital in the world at that time. And the Xingjiao Temple Pagoda on Shaoling Plain south of Chang'an — the site of Master Xuanzang's relic pagoda — bears witness to Chang'an's glory as a Buddhist center. From the Rainbow Skirt and Feathered Coat of Xingqing Palace to the morning bells and evening drums of Xingjiao Temple, Chang'an's diversity and包容 need no further words.

stops.title: Stop 3: Giant Wild Goose Pagoda — Winding Stream Banquets and Pagoda Inscriptions
stops.content: The Giant Wild Goose Pagoda appears under the name 'Daci'en Temple' in the Chang'an Gazetteer. Song Minqiu recorded: 'Daci'en Temple is in Jinchang Ward, originally the Jingjue Temple of the Sui, built in the twenty-second year of the Tang Zhenguan era.' He particularly noted: 'The temple has a stupa, which is the Giant Wild Goose Pagoda, built by Xuanzang to house the scriptures and images.' — concise and clear. The Giant Wild Goose Pagoda was the cultural landmark of Tang Chang'an. Every spring, after the newly successful jinshi graduates passed the examinations, the court hosted a banquet on the banks of the Qujiang River — 'Winding Stream Banquet' — and then brought the new graduates to inscribe their names at the foot of the Giant Wild Goose Pagoda. Song Minqiu wrote: 'Those who passed the jinshi examination inscribed their names on the Ci'en Temple pagoda' — 'Wild Goose Pagoda Inscription' became the most glorious dream of Chinese literati. Bai Juyi, when he passed the jinshi at twenty-seven, proudly wrote: 'At the inscription site beneath Ci'en Pagoda, among seventeen, the youngest was I.' Today, the Giant Wild Goose Pagoda remains Xi'an's landmark, its musical fountain dancing every evening. But Song Minqiu's Chang'an Gazetteer tells us that this pagoda's true moment of glory was when scholars who had studied for ten years by the cold window finally carved their names where they were closest to the sky. Song Minqiu recorded the architectural dimensions of the Giant Wild Goose Pagoda in detail: 'The pagoda was originally five stories, then collapsed and was rebuilt during the Chang'an era of Empress Wu, increased to ten stories. Later damaged by fire, it was reduced to seven stories.' — he accurately traced the pagoda's changes from five stories to ten and then to seven. Today's Giant Wild Goose Pagoda stands 64.5 meters tall, with a base side length of 25 meters, a model of imitation-wood brick pagoda architecture in China. Each of its four sides has arched doors, with exquisite line-carved Buddha images on the lintels — the Buddha hall image on the west-face lintel of the ground floor is the earliest surviving Tang timber-architecture image material in China, of inestimable academic value. The Giant Wild Goose Pagoda also bears a more touching name — 'Ci'en Pagoda.' Ci'en Temple was built by Emperor Gaozong of Tang to pray for his mother, Empress Wende. The name 'Ci'en' is steeped in filial devotion. After returning from his pilgrimage, Master Xuanzang translated scriptures here for nineteen years, producing seventy-five texts in 1,335 fascicles, more than half of the total new Buddhist translations of the Tang dynasty. 'At the inscription site beneath Ci'en Pagoda, among seventeen, the youngest was I' — Bai Juyi's pride is still carved on the steles beneath the pagoda, and Song Minqiu's Chang'an Gazetteer gives every number and every story of this pagoda its origin.

stops.title: Stop 4: Small Wild Goose Pagoda — Three Splits and Three Reunions at Jianfu Temple
stops.content: The Small Wild Goose Pagoda appears under the name 'Jianfu Temple' in the Chang'an Gazetteer. Song Minqiu recorded: 'Jianfu Temple is in Kaihua Ward, built in the first year of the Wenming era.' The Small Wild Goose Pagoda is the Buddhist pagoda of Jianfu Temple, smaller than the Giant Wild Goose Pagoda, a thirteen-story dense-eave brick pagoda, elegant and simple. The Small Wild Goose Pagoda's most legendary feature is its 'three splits and three reunions' — it split open due to earthquakes three times in history, and three times closed back together during subsequent quakes. Song Minqiu, a Northern Song man, may have recorded the first account of the pagoda splitting after its completion. During the Ming Chenghua and Zhengde eras, two major earthquakes occurred, and each time the pagoda miraculously 'closed itself.' The ancients considered this 'divine protection,' while modern engineering analysis attributes it to 'hemispherical foundation stress distribution' — but regardless of the explanation, this thirteen-hundred-year-old brick pagoda still stands in Xi'an today, itself a miracle. Song Minqiu also paid special attention to the bell of Jianfu Temple — 'The temple bell, struck at dawn and dusk, its sound carries for tens of li.' Like the Small Wild Goose Pagoda itself, this bell sound has also traversed a millennium. The Small Wild Goose Pagoda's dense-eave form is extremely rare in the Guanzhong region —层层叠涩 projecting eaves, with wind bells hanging at the eaves corners tinkling in the breeze. On the south face of the pagoda hangs a Qing-dynasty 'divine bell,' cast in thick iron, whose toll rings throughout the city — this is the origin of 'Wild Goose Pagoda Morning Bell.' Song Minqiu wrote: 'The temple bell, struck at dawn and dusk, its sound carries for tens of li' — even in the Northern Song, the Small Wild Goose Pagoda's bell was already the most melodious time signal in Chang'an city. Tang-dynasty Jianfu Temple held a extremely prominent地位 — Emperor Zhongzong of Tang established the 'Scripture Translation Institute' here, inviting Master Yijing to translate the Buddhist scriptures he had brought back from India. Yijing, one of the three great Tang-dynasty Tripitaka masters alongside Xuanzang, translated scriptures at Jianfu Temple for seven years, producing important texts such as the Suvarnaprabhasa Sutra. The Small Wild Goose Pagoda kept company with the Scripture Translation Institute, its candlelight never extinguished through the night — it was the brightest cultural beacon in the night sky of the Great Tang. Today, the Small Wild Goose Pagoda has become one with the Xi'an Museum, the ancient locust tree before it still lush, its shade filled with people drinking tea and chatting — Chang'an's bell is no longer an imperial privilege but a city's breath.

stops.title: Stop 5: Qinglong Temple — The Last Cherry Blossoms in Chang'an City
stops.content: Qinglong Temple was one of the most important esoteric Buddhist monasteries in Tang Chang'an, located in Xinchang Ward. Song Minqiu wrote in the Chang'an Gazetteer: 'Qinglong Temple is in Xinchang Ward, built as Linggan Temple in the Sui, renamed Qinglong Temple in the second year of the Tang Jingyun era.' Six of the eight famous Japanese monks who studied in Tang China studied at Qinglong Temple — most notably the monk Kukai (Kobo Daishi), who studied under Master Huiguo at Qinglong Temple, and after returning to Japan founded the Shingon school of Buddhism. By Song Minqiu's time, Qinglong Temple was already abandoned — after the fall of the Tang, Chang'an city drastically shrank, and the eastern district where Qinglong Temple stood became farmland. But Song Minqiu faithfully recorded its location and history. In the twentieth century, archaeologists used the Chang'an Gazetteer's records to excavate the Qinglong Temple site in the eastern suburbs of Xi'an. Today, the temple has been reconstructed on the site, and every spring when the cherry blossoms bloom, it is the most romantic place in Xi'an. Those cherry trees were mostly donated by Japanese friends — descendants of Kukai use cherry blossoms to commemorate the beautiful chapter of Sino-Japanese cultural exchange 1,200 years ago. If Song Minqiu knew of this in the underworld, he would probably add a note to his Qinglong Temple entry: 'Today there are cherry blossoms, fragrant flowers filling the temple.' Qinglong Temple's status in Tang Chang'an ranked alongside Ci'en Temple and Jianfu Temple. Song Minqiu recorded: 'Qinglong Temple was originally Linggan Temple of the Sui, renamed Qinglong Temple in the second year of the Jingyun era (711).' Tang-dynasty esoteric master Huiguo presided here for a long time, 'his dharma heirs numbered no fewer than a thousand.' The most famous among them was the Japanese monk Kukai — he came to Tang China in the twentieth year of the Zhenyuan era (804) to seek the dharma, studied esoteric Buddhism under Huiguo, and within less than two years received the abhisheka title 'Vajra Light All-Pervading.' After returning to Japan, he founded the Shingon school. The three characters 'Qinglong Temple' hold a status in Japanese Buddhism akin to 'the Buddha's homeland' — every year tens of thousands of Japanese devotees make pilgrimages here. The archaeological discoveries at the Qinglong Temple site have been extremely important — in 1981, excavations unearthed the middle gate, pagoda base, cloisters, and other foundation structures, along with大量 Tang-dynasty tile-ends and fragmentary clay Buddhas, fully restoring the layout of a Tang esoteric monastery. The site is now part of the Sui Daxing and Tang Chang'an City Site — because the 'Xinchang Ward' where Qinglong Temple was located was near the east city wall of Tang Chang'an, one of the most prosperous wards outside the 'Eastern Market.' From Qinglong Temple's cherry blossoms to Kukai's kasaya, from Huiguo's abhisheka to the ink traces of the Chang'an Gazetteer — the rise and fall of a single monastery has touched the pulse of the entire East Asian cultural sphere.

stops.title: Stop 6: Xi'an Stele Forest — A Library on Stone
stops.content: When Song Minqiu wrote the Chang'an Gazetteer, the Xi'an Stele Forest had not yet taken its present form. But he had already noticed the large number of stelae and stone carvings in Tang Chang'an — the Kaicheng Stone Classics, the Stone Platform Filial Piety Classic, the Nestorian Stele, and others. He wrote: 'Chang'an's stone inscriptions are the finest under heaven.' After the Song dynasty, people gathered scattered stelae together for preservation, gradually forming today's Xi'an Stele Forest — the earliest and richest collection of ancient stone inscriptions in China. Over four thousand stelae, from the Han to the Qing, encompass all calligraphic styles — seal, clerical, standard, running, and cursive script — Yan Zhenqing's Duobao Pagoda Stele, Liu Gongquan's Mysterious Pagoda Stele, Wang Xizhi's Preface to the Sacred Teachings... every stele is a peak in calligraphic history. If the Chang'an Gazetteer used words to restore Chang'an, then the Xi'an Stele Forest used stone to preserve Chang'an. Song Minqiu turned paper pages; we look at stone. Chang'an was always there, merely changed in form. Song Minqiu said in his preface to the Chang'an Gazetteer: 'A gazetteer is made to guard against forgetfulness.' — he feared that later generations would forget Chang'an. We can tell him: No, never. Song Minqiu could not have foreseen that eight hundred years after his death, the Xi'an Stele Forest would become one of the world's most important treasuries of calligraphic art. The Kaicheng Stone Classics he noted — carved in the second year of the Tang Wenzong Kaicheng era (837), 114 stelae, over 650,000 characters of the complete Confucian canon — remain the Stele Forest's greatest treasure, the largest stone-engraved textbook in ancient China. Song Minqiu specifically noted in the Chang'an Gazetteer: 'The Kaicheng Stone Classics were erected at the Imperial Academy, comprising the twelve classics of the Book of Changes, Book of Documents, Poetry, Zhou Rites, Ceremonial Rites, Record of Rites, Spring and Autumn Annals with Zuo Commentary, Gongyang Commentary, Guliang Commentary, Filial Piety Classic, Analects, and Erya' — he listed each classic accurately, as if cataloging this library on stone. The famous calligraphic stelae in the Stele Forest are breathtaking: Yan Zhenqing's Duobao Pagoda Stele and Yan Family Temple Stele, Liu Gongquan's Mysterious Pagoda Stele, Ouyang Xun's Huangfu Dan Stele, Chu Suiliang's Tongzhou Preface to the Sacred Teachings... the most brilliant dances of the brush, eternally定格 on stone. Most moving of all is Wang Xizhi's Preface to the Sacred Teachings of the Great Tang Tripitaka — though this is a 'assembled-character stele' compiled over twenty-four years by the Tang monk Huairen using Wang's characters, Wang's brushwork — 'drifting like clouds, startling like dragons' — is intact. Song Minqiu spent his life with words. If he walked into today's Stele Forest Museum, he would probably, just as he once pored over Tang documents in his study, touch each cold stone — except this time, he would finally be touching Chang'an itself.
